lesson.title: The Dental Hardening (TH → D)
lesson.subtitle: The shift that connects think, thank, and brother

foreshadow.line: You have just watched th become d. Something bigger is hiding in that D: three of the most common words in German are built out of it, and they are not verbs at all. Hold the thought.

hook.title: Why German Has No 'TH' Sound
hook.content: Notice how native German speakers learning English often struggle with the 'th' sound? That is because German completely abolished dental fricatives over 1,300 years ago. Every single original Germanic 'th' sound hardened directly into 'd'. You already own proof from the wild: danke — the one German word everyone picks up — is thank with its th hardened to d.

footnotes.title: Dental Hardening
footnotes.content: The voiced dental fricative [ð] and voiceless [θ] hardened into the stop [d] across all High German dialects.

pattern.title: English TH = German D
pattern.content: Every English 'TH' hardens to 'D' in German. Think becomes denken. Thank becomes danken (notice English has the exact same vowel pair: think and thank!). Three becomes drei. Brother becomes Bruder. Thing becomes Ding (Norse and Germanic assemblies were called 'Things', where matters were discussed). Bath becomes Bad (as in famous German spa towns like Baden-Baden). Roof/thatch becomes Dach. Thou/thee becomes du/dich.

footnotes.title: Thou/Thee & Donner
footnotes.content: English 'thou' (thou goest) and German 'du' (du gehst) both take the ancient -st ending. Santa's reindeer 'Donner and Blitzen' literally means 'Thunder and Lightning' (Donnerstag = Thunder-day / Thursday)!

pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “German D is just English D with an accent.” It is not. The German D that comes from English th is a new letter doing the old job — read it as English D and you will miss denken for think and Dank for thank. Say the English th first, then let it harden.
pattern.linguist_note: Unlike the P→F shift, which was geographically restricted to High German, the TH→D shift eventually reached even northern Low German and Dutch, leaving English and Icelandic as the lone survivors of Germanic 'th'.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German verb for 'to thank' using the TH → D rule:
exercises.affirmation: You hardened the th into d and hung on the -en — thank is danken now, all the way down.
exercises.explanation: Dental TH hardened to D + infinitive suffix -en = danken.

exercises.prompt: Match the English TH words to their German D counterparts:
exercises.affirmation: Four th-words hardened to d on sight — a 1,300-year-old rule, live in your hands.
exercises.explanation: Every Germanic dental fricative TH hardened into D in German.

exercises.prompt: What native English word shares the exact root of 'Bruder'?
exercises.affirmation: You ran the d → th swap and brother stepped out — that medial d is hardened th.
exercises.explanation: Medial D in Bruder directly mirrors English TH in brother.

exercises.prompt: Apply the TH → D shift: English: 'think' → German verb:
exercises.affirmation: You hardened th to d and let the -en settle — think became denken.
exercises.explanation: TH shifts to D, plus regular -en infinitive.

exercises.idea: you're letting someone far away know they're on your mind: I think of you
cues: Who thinks? → ich denke (TH → D: think → denk-)
'of you' → an dich — denken needs its an, and thee → dich
Line them up: thinker, an, then the thee-word

vocab_hints.note: direct twin of archaic English 'thee' (thou ↔ du, thee ↔ dich, thine ↔ dein)

exercises.explanation: 'denken an' takes the accusative (dich = thee). Notice TH → D: think ↔ denke, thee ↔ dich.

summary.outcome: Recognize several English th and German d cognates in familiar words and phrases.
summary.takeaway: Whenever you encounter a German 'd', swap it for 'th' in your head to unlock the English cognate.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Donner, Bad & Du — culture words through the D-lens: thunder-day, spa towns, and the thou you already speak.

twist.prompt: Same thought, but the whole family says it: I think of you becomes we think of you.
twist.explanation: ich denke → wir denken: the ending carries the person (-e → -en), and 'an dich' doesn't budge. The shift words stay; the endings do the work.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

bruder.etymology_derivation: Medial th shifted to d; unstressed -er vocalizes to [ɐ].

bad.etymology_derivation: Final th shifted to d (devoiced in pronunciation to [t]). Verb: baden (to bathe).

donner.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Living in English "Thursday" (Thor's/Thunder's day = Donnerstag) and Santa's reindeer "Donner and Blitzen" (Thunder and Lightning).

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

backen.context_phrase: Ich backe einen Kuchen für dich.
backen.context_translation: I'm baking a cake for you.
backen.etymology_derivation: Old High German backan — explicit cognate of English bake (see der Bäcker). [wiktionary]

limonade.context_phrase: Im Sommer trinke ich gern Limonade.
limonade.context_translation: In summer I like to drink lemonade.
limonade.etymology_derivation: Limonade — borrowed from French limonade, the same drink-word English took as lemonade; the lemon itself traveled from Asia through Persian and Arabic. [wiktionary]

wild.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz — the exact twin of English wild; the English entry on the same page names German wild as its cognate. [wiktionary]

spinne.etymology_derivation: From Old High German spinna, an agent noun from the verb spinnen, to spin. Archaic English spinner is the listed cognate, and English spider is built on the same spin root. [wiktionary]

doch.english_cognate: yet; after all (particle: on the contrary)
doch.english_meaning: yet; after all (particle: on the contrary)
doch.context_phrase: Das Essen war teuer, doch sehr lecker.
doch.context_translation: The food was expensive, yet very tasty.
doch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þauh — the exact twin of English though (Old English þēah); English kept th, German hardened it to d, the classic dental shift. [wiktionary]

dennoch.context_phrase: Sie ist müde, dennoch lernt sie weiter.
dennoch.context_translation: She is tired, nevertheless she keeps studying.
dennoch.etymology_derivation: Denn (then — the th-to-d twin of English then) plus noch (still, yet); literally then-yet, nevertheless. [wiktionary]

schwiegervater.etymology_derivation: Schwieger- + Vater; the Vater element is the twin of English father (th to d, from PIE *ph₂tḗr). The old element Schwieger- has no surviving English twin. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
